entries.title: Who is Stephen Miller, Trump’s new White House chief of staff?
entries.summary: Miller has been a close confidant of Trump since 2016 and an architect of the president's hardline immigration policies.
entries.content:
Miller has been a close confidant of Trump since 2016 and an architect of the president’s hardline immigration policies.

United States President Donald Trump has tapped his longtime adviser Stephen Miller to be White House chief of staff.

The move on Friday represented a doubling down on Trump’s most controversial policies following his Republican Party’s midterm drubbing earlier this week.

Democrats will take control of the US House of Representatives and Senate in January, and are widely expected to launch investigations into Miller’s role in the White House.

The 41-year-old Miller has been one of Trump’s most vocal defenders and is widely seen as an architect of the president’s mass deportation campaign.

In his post on Truth Social, Trump called Miller “one of my most trusted advisors”, saying he would take over the role from Susie Wiles on Monday.

An early adherent

Miller had built a reputation as a conservative activist long before entering Trump’s orbit.

At Santa Monica High School, he cut his teeth railing against what he described as liberal school policies on local radio shows.

At Duke University, he led the Duke Conservative Union and became a staunch advocate for three of the school’s lacrosse players after they were accused of rape.

After college, he moved to Washington, DC, where he worked as a legislative aide to Republican members of Congress and Republican Senator Jeff Sessions.

He joined Trump’s initial presidential campaign in January 2016, where he was credited with shaping the president’s messaging and caustic political stylings.

“I think he and Trump hit it off from the very beginning,” former Trump adviser Steve Bannon told The Associated Press news agency in 2017. “I think he helped Trump find his voice.”

What was his role during Trump’s first term?

Following Trump’s surprise victory in the 2016 race, Miller assumed the role of presidential adviser and speechwriter.

He served as an influential voice in shaping Trump’s most strident actions related to immigration, often framing the issues as an effort to protect Western “civilisation”.

During that period, Democratic lawmakers accused Miller of perpetuating white nationalist rhetoric.

In 2019, the Southern Poverty Law Center released emails allegedly showing the Trump adviser supporting white nationalist websites and ideologies. That spurred a renewed push from Democratic lawmakers, who sought Miller’s removal from the White House.

“It is unacceptable for the Trump Administration to knowingly install a known white nationalist and believer of white supremacist ideology in a position of power and influence over federal policy,” Congress member Joaquin Castro said in a statement in 2020.

Miller is credited with shaping the Department of Justice’s 2018 “Zero Tolerance” policy at the US border, which called for the arrest of nearly every adult crossing into the US without legal documentation.

The scheme resulted in widespread family separation, with children barred from being housed in criminal detention facilities along with their parents. Trump later changed the policy via executive order, amid widespread outrage.

As an adviser to Trump, Miller campaigned to end Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA), a programme that allowed individuals brought to the US as children without documentation to receive legal paperwork for education and employment. The programme stopped accepting new applicants in 2021.

Miller also drove wide-scale visa restrictions during Trump’s first term, including a 2017 travel ban on several Muslim-majority countries, which came to be known as the “Muslim travel ban”.

The initial order blocked citizens of Syria, Iran, Iraq, Libya, Somalia, Sudan and Yemen from entering the US for 90 days. An adjusted version of the policy was eventually upheld by the US Supreme Court.

He later became a top proponent of Trump’s unfounded claims that the 2020 election was stolen, supporting a scheme for Trump to be certified as the victor.

Trump 2.0

Miller remained by Trump’s side as the former president staged a political comeback ahead of the 2024 presidential vote. He became Trump’s deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser when the administration retook office in January 2025.

Since then, he has helped to orchestrate Trump’s mass deportation drive, which has seen immigration enforcement agents flood communities across the country, increasingly targeting individuals with no or only minor criminal records.

In May 2025, Miller told Fox News the administration had “set a goal of a minimum of 3,000 arrests for ICE every day, and President Trump is going to keep pushing to get that number up higher each and every day”.

He has also been a vocal defender of increasingly violent tactics by immigration agents. He initially defended the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by immigration agents in Minneapolis in January, calling them both “terrorists” before walking back the statement about Pretti.

As part of Trump’s deportation efforts, the administration has sought to expel visa-holders and permanent residents who have been supportive of Palestinian rights and critical of the Israeli government’s abuses in places like Gaza and the West Bank.

The Trump administration has argued that such views are harmful to US foreign policy. Miller’s role in that crafting that argument has come under scrutiny in recent months.

In July, Mahmoud Khalil, a former graduate student at Columbia University, filed a lawsuit against several Trump administration officials, including Miller, accusing them of orchestrating “a conspiracy to single out Mr Khalil and other non-citizen Palestinians”.

Khalil continues to face deportation proceedings under Trump for his role in pro-Palestinian protests.

In the past, Miller has criticised pro-Palestinian voices, like that of US Representative Rashida Tlaib, considered the first Palestinian American woman to serve in Congress.

“Rashida Tlaib should be expelled from Congress,” Miller told Fox News in 2023, as he proceeded to call the representative and other Democrats “deeply anti-Semitic and deeply anti-American”.

In his return to the White House, Miller also unsuccessfully sought to end birthright citizenship, while becoming an increasingly vocal defender of Trump’s military actions in the Western Hemisphere.

He endorsed the US abduction of Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro and told CNN in January that the US had a right to seize Greenland based on its military might.

“We live in a world in which you can talk all you want about international niceties and everything else, but we live in a world, in the real world … that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power,” he said.

“These are the iron laws of the world that have existed since the beginning of time.”

What does a chief of staff do?

It was not immediately clear how Miller’s new role would affect his influence over Trump.

The chief of staff is typically tasked with overseeing White House staff and hiring, maintaining the president’s calendar, and advising the president on policy.

Some insiders refer to the role, which largely controls information flows, as the “gatekeeper” to the presidency.

entries.title: Protesters break into Microsoft data centre site in Amsterdam
entries.summary: Data centres face protests across Europe due to the massive amounts of computing power and water they use.
entries.content:
Data centres face protests across Europe due to the massive amounts of computing power and water they use.

Protesters in the Netherlands have broken into a construction site for a new Microsoft data centre in Amsterdam, the latest action in a growing movement sweeping Europe.

Several hundred activists occupied the site in the Sloterdijk district on Friday, responding to a call for a two-day protest across Europe against data centres, which handle the large processing workloads associated with artificial intelligence (AI). Demonstrators clashed with police as some climbed a crane and set off flares.

Nathan Timmer, of the protest group Geef Tegengas – which translates as Push Back – told local broadcaster AT5 that demonstrators were occupying the site in an effort to stop construction.

“We don’t want it to be built. Nobody needs it,” Timmer said. “The only thing this will be used for is AI slop. AI warfare, data surveillance and committing genocide. We don’t want that.”

Pro-Palestinian activists also joined the demonstrations in the Dutch capital. By late afternoon police were escorting activists off the construction site, though some remained, local media reported.

Dutch police said they detained 150-200 people suspected of trespassing during the protest.

Microsoft said it was aware of the Amsterdam demonstration.

“We understand that people feel strongly about the project, and we respect their right to express those views peacefully,” a spokesperson said. “However, we do not condone any actions that are unlawful or that put people’s safety at risk.”

Data centres face resistance around the world due to the massive amounts of computing power and water they use. Activists argue that the boom in facilities serving cloud computing and AI is moving faster than public consultation and environmental oversight.

Dozens of civil society and grassroots groups have said they will join the “Stop Dirty Data Centres” events on Friday and Saturday in 15 European countries, including Ireland, Poland, Denmark, Finland, Spain, Italy, the Netherlands, France and the United Kingdom, organisers said.

In Germany, a dozen protesters gathered in front of a data centre on the outskirts of Berlin on Friday.

“We want to put a stop to this blind construction of data centres around Germany, regardless of any environmental concerns,” said protest spokeswoman Caro Weber. “This is really, really dangerous for our future.”

About 100 people also protested against data centres in front of the Polish parliament, representing communities around Warsaw where new centres are planned.

In Italy, the fast-growing data centre industry is facing an equally rapid rise in grassroots opposition, particularly in the northern Lombardy region, the country’s main hub for digital infrastructure.

entries.title: Meghan Markle’s father arrested in US over alleged child sex abuse photos
entries.summary: US authorities found sexually explicit photos that appeared to show Thomas Markle with prepubescent girls.
entries.content:
US authorities found sexually explicit photos that appeared to show Thomas Markle with prepubescent girls.

The estranged father of Britain’s Prince Harry’s wife, Meghan Markle, has been arrested in the United States on a charge of possession of child sexual abuse material.

The US Department of Justice on Friday announced that Thomas Markle Sr was arrested in Florida after law enforcement officers discovered “sexually explicit photographs” of him with prepubescent girls in two storage units, located in the Los Angeles area, that he rented for nearly two decades.

“Mr Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions”, Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) Director Kash Patel said on Thursday.

According to the Justice Department, authorities learned in October that an individual signed an affidavit stating they had discovered child sex abuse material among Markle’s possessions in the Philippines.

Law enforcement interviewed a separate individual who told them the 82-year-old had rented a storage unit near Los Angeles since 2008. Information gathered from the first individual led to the discovery of a second unit.

After receiving warrants, the Justice Department said FBI agents searched the two units registered to Thomas. Inside, they found 78 items, including photos, film negatives and books that contained explicit imagery of him with underage girls.

The affidavit described three of those photographs. Two showed a man, who a witness identified as Thomas, with a nude prepubescent girl. The third photo shows a nude underage girl in what appeared to be a Philippine hotel room.

Officials, according to the affidavit, also found photos that appeared to show Thomas with “children in various stages of undress”.

Thomas was living in the Philippines earlier this year when he suffered a stroke and had his left leg amputated. That forced him to return to the US.

‘Deeply distressed’

Meghan issued a statement to The New York Times in October, saying she first learned of the allegations against her father in 2018, when a letter detailing them was sent to the unit of London’s Metropolitan Police that was handling her security then.

“I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours,” the duchess of Sussex wrote to the Times in an apparent reference to reports by the Sun, a British tabloid, on the allegations. “My thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.”

“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them,” she added.

The arrest of Thomas comes as President Donald Trump’s administration has been criticised for its handling of cases related to the abuse of children, particularly the release of files on the investigation into convicted sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein.

Last year, King Charles stripped Prince Andrew of his princely title as he tried to shield the royal family from the scandal surrounding his brother’s relationship with Epstein.

Meghan, Prince Harry and their two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, relocated back to the United Kingdom in August.

The Associated Press tried to reach Meghan’s representative on Friday but has not yet heard back.

Thomas Markle is expected to appear in a Florida court on Friday. If convicted, the Justice Department said he could face a maximum sentence of 20 years in a US federal prison.

entries.title: Pope Leo arrives in Uruguay starting 12-day Latin America tour
entries.summary: The 71-year-old pontiff is visiting three countries despite undergoing surgery to remove a tumour last month.
entries.content:
The 71-year-old pontiff is visiting three countries despite undergoing surgery to remove a tumour last month.

Pope Leo XIV has arrived in Uruguay as he begins a 12-day tour of South America, three weeks after undergoing lung cancer surgery that had put the entire trip into question.

The 71-year-old head of the Roman Catholic Church touched down in Montevideo on Friday after a 13-hour flight from Rome, telling reporters he feels “fairly good”.

“I know some people were doubtful about this trip taking place,” Leo told reporters on board the papal plane. “I had no doubt and was convinced that this trip had to go forward. And I am very happy to say praise the Lord and thanks to wonderful medical assistance, I’m here today, I think in fairly good shape.”

On his trip, the pope is scheduled to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in one of the most intense papal foreign trips in decades.

His packed three-day itinerary in Uruguay – the region’s least Catholic and most secular country – will include a visit to a neighbourhood with heavy gang violence, a mass in Paysandu, about 375 kilometres (230 miles) from Montevideo, and another mass in the city of Florida, about 100 kilometres (60 miles) from the capital.

Cardinal Daniel Sturla, archbishop of Montevideo, told the AFP news agency that there was “widespread interest in the pope’s visit that goes well beyond the confines of the Catholic Church”, with tickets for masses in Paysandu and Florida quickly running out.

The regional trip is somewhat of a homecoming journey for Leo, as he will finish in Peru in three weeks, where he served for almost two decades as a missionary, forming a deep attachment to the continent.

The trip will take the pope to the former Inca capital of Cusco and the Amazon rainforest, and he will also revisit his old diocese of Chiclayo for a private visit to a chapel he helped rebuild.

Leo said on Wednesday that he was looking forward to returning to a region “so dear to me”.

The leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics said he hoped the trip would “strengthen faith, renew hope, and rekindle the fire of charity” in the countries he is visiting, which face rising inequality and violence, as well as a decline in Catholic followers.

Despite undergoing an operation on October 13 to remove a cancerous tumour, doctors have given him the all-clear to travel, and the Vatican said no special medical measures were necessary beyond the standard care on papal trips.

“His stamina is fantastic. The way that he’s singing is incredible. And you can only sing if your lungs are really strong,” said Maria Montserrat Alvarado, the Vatican’s new communications chief. She noted that Leo had passed the 14-day convalescence period required by doctors after his surgery and was eager to get on the road.
